cls: Topical antipsoriatic (anthracene derivative); also known as anthralin
pharm: Reduces the abnormally rapid epidermal cell proliferation of psoriasis and has anti-inflammatory and antioxidant-modulating actions in the skin
quick: Apply to plaques once daily starting at 0.1%, increasing strength as tolerated (often short-contact 0.1-2%)
Limited data; use only if clearly needed, on limited areas
Avoid application to the breast; otherwise minimal systemic absorption
Skin response and irritation; protect uninvolved skin and avoid the face/flexures/eyes
summary: Dithranol (anthralin) is a topical anthracene derivative used to treat chronic plaque psoriasis. It reduces the excessive proliferation of keratinocytes characteristic of psoriasis and exerts anti-inflammatory effects, in part through modulation of cellular oxidative processes and mitochondrial function. It is NOT currently in the openFDA label database (largely discontinued/limited in the US); this record is based on EU/SmPC and BNF-type information. It is applied to psoriatic plaques, classically using either a graded conventional regimen (left on overnight) or, more commonly now, short-contact therapy (applied for 10-60 minutes then washed off), starting at a low concentration (e.g. 0.1%) and increasing as tolerated. Its main drawbacks are skin irritation/burning of surrounding normal skin and a characteristic brown-purple staining of skin, hair, nails, clothing and surfaces. It must be kept off the face, flexures, genitalia and eyes, and surrounding uninvolved skin should be protected.
indications: Chronic stable plaque psoriasis (subacute and chronic plaques)
Used in both conventional (overnight) and short-contact regimens, including as part of the Ingram regimen with UVB

dosage.d: Apply to plaques once daily, starting at 0.1%, increasing strength stepwise (up to 1-2% or higher) as tolerated; leave on 10-60 minutes then wash off
dosage.n: Increase contact time/strength gradually to balance efficacy and irritation

dosage.d: Apply a lower strength to plaques and leave in place (e.g. overnight), increasing concentration as tolerated
dosage.n: Protect surrounding skin; often used with paste and dressings in hospital settings

dosage.n: Wash hands after use; protect surrounding skin with soft paraffin if needed

admin: Apply carefully and only to the psoriatic plaques, avoiding normal/uninvolved skin
Keep away from the face, skin folds (flexures), genitalia and especially the eyes
Protect surrounding healthy skin (e.g. with white soft paraffin) to limit irritation and staining
For short-contact therapy, leave on for the prescribed time (often 10-60 minutes) then wash off thoroughly
Start at a low concentration and increase strength/contact time gradually according to tolerance
Wash hands immediately after application; expect staining of skin, hair, nails, fabrics and bathware
moa: Dithranol acts locally in the epidermis to normalise the accelerated keratinocyte turnover of psoriasis. It is taken up into epidermal cells where it is thought to impair mitochondrial function and DNA synthesis and to generate reactive oxygen species that modulate cell proliferation and inflammation, reducing the hyperproliferation of psoriatic plaques. It also has anti-inflammatory effects on immune cells in the skin. Systemic absorption through intact and psoriatic skin is minimal, so its actions and adverse effects are essentially confined to the site of application.

absolute: Acute, pustular, erythrodermic or unstable (inflamed) psoriasis
Application to the face, eyes, mucous membranes, flexures or genitalia
relative: Renal impairment (caution with extensive application, theoretical)

preg: Systemic absorption of dithranol is minimal, but data in pregnancy are limited. Use only if clearly needed, applied sparingly to limited plaque areas, and avoid extensive use.
lact: Because of negligible systemic absorption, topical dithranol is generally considered low risk during breastfeeding, but it should not be applied to the breast/nipple area to avoid infant skin contact.
renal: No dose adjustment is required because systemic absorption is negligible; caution is theoretical only with very extensive application.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required because systemic absorption is negligible.

moderate: Other topical irritants or keratolytics (e.g. salicylic acid, topical retinoids) applied to the same area - additive irritation
Topical corticosteroids - may be combined under specialist guidance
minor: UV phototherapy (e.g. UVB in the Ingram regimen) - used therapeutically together but increases skin sensitivity
interactions.diagnostics: No effect on laboratory tests; causes visible brown-purple staining of skin/nails

common: Skin irritation, burning or stinging at and around the application site
Brown-purple staining of skin, hair and nails
Staining of clothing, bedding, baths and surfaces
serious: Severe localised chemical burn/dermatitis if applied incorrectly or to normal skin
Severe conjunctival/corneal irritation if it contacts the eyes
emergency: Severe eye contamination causing intense irritation (requires immediate irrigation and review)

monitoring: Local skin tolerance (irritation, burning) at each strength increase
Avoidance of spread onto normal skin
counsel: Apply only to the thickened psoriasis patches, not the normal skin around them
Keep it well away from your eyes, face, skin folds and genitals; wash hands straight after applying

For short-contact use, leave it on only for the time advised, then wash it off thoroughly
Some stinging or redness is expected; tell your doctor if the skin becomes very sore or blistered
The skin staining fades over a couple of weeks after stopping treatment
pk: Improvement in plaques over days to a few weeks of regular use
Acts locally in the epidermis; negligible systemic absorption
Local effect persists with continued application; staining fades over ~2 weeks after stopping
Store in a cool place, protect from light and air (oxidises and discolours); keep tightly closed
pearls: NOT in the FDA label database / largely discontinued in the US (also called anthralin) - this record is from EU/SmPC and BNF sources
Effective, non-steroidal topical for chronic plaque psoriasis; staining and irritation limit its use
Short-contact therapy (apply 10-60 min then wash off) reduces staining/irritation versus overnight use
Start low (0.1%) and increase strength/contact time gradually as tolerated
Strictly avoid the face, flexures, genitalia and eyes; protect surrounding normal skin
Causes characteristic brown-purple staining of skin, nails, hair, fabrics and bathware (skin stain fades after stopping)
missed: If you miss an application, apply it when you remember, or skip it and resume your usual schedule if it is almost time for the next one - do not apply a double amount. Consistent daily use gives the best results.
overdose: Topical overdose (excessive amount, strength or contact time) mainly causes intense local irritation or a chemical burn. Wash off thoroughly, treat the affected skin as a localised burn/dermatitis, and reduce strength or contact time on resuming. Accidental ingestion is unlikely to be serious but warrants symptomatic care and poison-centre advice; eye contact requires immediate copious irrigation and ophthalmic review.
